snippet.title: The Battle That Made Alexander a God — The Battle of Issus (333 BC)
snippet.description:
This video respectfully explores the moment when Alexander the Great faced the mighty Persian Empire — and forever changed how the world saw him. At Issus, against impossible odds, a young king confronted Darius III and emerged not just as a conqueror, but as a living legend.

In this video, discover how:
• Alexander used terrain and speed to defeat a far larger army
• The clash at Issus shattered the myth of Persian invincibility
• Darius III’s flight reshaped the psychology of the ancient world
• This single battle elevated Alexander from king to godlike figure
• Issus became a turning point in the history of empire and warfare

The Battle of Issus was more than a military victory — it was a moment of myth-making, where strategy, courage, and destiny collided on the battlefield.

snippet.title: The Most Famous Unit in Ancient History Had the Wrong Name
snippet.description:
The most feared unit name in ancient history was a mistranslation.
The Persians called them anûšiya — companions. The Greek historian Herodotus confused this with anauša — immortal. The name stuck. The reality was different.
At Thermopylae in 480 BC, after two days of failed assaults by regular Persian infantry, Xerxes sent his companions into the pass. Ten thousand men, every one glittering with gold carried on their person. Colorful patterned tunics concealing fish-scale iron plates underneath. Felt caps pulled low against the dust. Wicker shields. Short spears with silver pomegranate counterweights — gold for the inner thousand, marking rank from the spear tip alone.
Behind them: a private caravan of wagons, camels, servants, and food reserved exclusively for their consumption. No other unit in the ancient world campaigned this way.
They entered the pass at Thermopylae.
They were repulsed. Twice. By the same Spartan line that had broken every other Persian formation that day.
They were replaced, as they always were. The number stayed at ten thousand.
Companions. Not immortals. The name was always wrong.

snippet.title: 1758: The Year the French Empire Collapsed in North America
snippet.description:
In July 1758, three British forces advanced on New France from every direction. To the east, General Amherst’s cannons thundered at the formidable fortress of Louisbourg as his men dug ever closer in a grueling siege. To the north, near Fort Ticonderoga, General Abercrombie’s troops emerged from the woods and launched a bold assault on the French defenses near Rattlesnake Hill. To the south, General John Forbes pressed westward toward Fort Duquesne, determined to drive the French from the contested Ohio Country. From the wilderness frontier to the strategic waterways of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, British forces were poised to breach the gates of New France, while at sea the Royal Navy slowly tightened its grip on Atlantic supply lines. The colony was under siege—beset on all fronts. While France was busy on the battlefields of Europe trying to keep the British Empire and Prussia at bay, Britain reached across oceans with ruthless precision, determined to crush the French Empire and tear it apart. This was no ordinary campaign. It was characterized by the bloodiest open-field battle of the French and Indian War, a classic Vauban-style siege, and a desperate race for indigenous and colonial support on the frontier. This is how modern historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of New France.

snippet.title: The Warrior Rome Spent 400 Years Trying to Copy
snippet.description:
On the morning of the Siege of Amida in 359 AD, Roman soldiers looked out from the city walls and saw mail-clad cavalry filling every hill and valley as far as the eye could reach. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus was on those walls. He wrote about what he saw for the rest of his life.
The Savaran were the heavy cavalry elite of the Sassanid Empire — the force that held Rome to a strategic draw for over four centuries. Their helmets enclosed the entire head in iron, fitted with the forms of human faces, leaving only two narrow slits for the eyes. Their full equipment load included a mail shirt to the knees, breastplate, arm guards, thigh guards, greaves, sword, lance, mace, axe, lasso, thirty arrows, and two bows. They had to be lifted onto their horses.
Before the charge closed, they fired the panjagan — five arrows in a single draw, creating localized kill zones before the first arrow had landed.
Amida fell after 73 days. Rome eventually copied Sassanid armor, Sassanid cavalry doctrine, and Sassanid tactical formations. The Savaran are the forgotten progenitors of the armored knight.

When Prince Louis of France invaded England in 1216, he met unexpected resistance deep in the dense forests of southern England. A man named William of Kensham, along with a group of partisans, struck fear into the hearts of the French. Much like the legendary Robin Hood and his daring companions, they lay in wait with their bows, attacking French knights whenever they ventured into the forest. Their weapons were cunning, surprise, and terror. They would appear out of nowhere, ambush a convoy, kill a few stragglers, and vanish silently into the shadows of the woods. 
William of Kensham and his men played a crucial role in repelling the French invasion during the First Barons’ War. They are among England’s unsung heroes—admired by their contemporaries but forgotten by history … almost, that is. Perhaps part of their legacy lives on in the legend of Robin Hood.

snippet.title: The Army of 150 Couples Who Broke Sparta
snippet.description:
The most fearless soldiers in ancient Greece were an army of lovers. And that was the whole point.
Thebes built an elite unit of 300 hand-picked warriors called the Sacred Band. They weren't 300 individuals. They were 150 pairs of lovers who swore to fight side by side.
The idea, written down by Plato, was ruthless: no man will run or show cowardice while the person he loves is watching. Shame is stronger than fear.
It worked. In 371 BC at Leuctra, they led the charge that shattered the Spartan army and broke the myth that Sparta couldn't be beaten.
For over thirty years, they were never defeated.
It ended at Chaeronea in 338 BC. The rest of the Greek line fled. The Sacred Band held, and died where they stood, in pairs.
Centuries later, archaeologists found them: 254 skeletons in neat rows, beneath a great stone lion that still stands today.

Outnumbered beyond hope, he launched a night campaign of terror near Târgoviște, using scorched earth, ambush, and intimidation to break the morale of the Ottoman advance and halt one of the most powerful armies on earth.

It is the true story behind the legend, where psychological warfare reshaped history and Europe’s fate hung in the balance.

snippet.title: America's *Other* Declaration of Independence & the Anti-Rent War | HISTORY This Week
snippet.description:
July 4, 1839. Sixty-three years after 1776—and centuries after the medieval period—feudalism is alive and well in the United States.

High on a rocky plain in upstate New York, a crowd of tenant farmers gathers in the village of Berne to read aloud a declaration of independence… but not the one you're thinking of. These families are still bound to a landlord by perpetual leases their grandfathers signed, owing bushels of wheat and a share of every sale for as long as the land exists. 

Today they're done. They call their leases "voluntary slavery" and vow to "take up the ball of the Revolution where our fathers stopped it." It's the opening shot of the Anti-Rent War,  a revolt that will pit disguised farmers against sheriffs and posses across the Hudson Valley, and force New York to ask whether a feudal bargain has any place in a republic. 

How did manor lords survive the Revolution? And what would it finally take to break their grip?

Special thanks Reeve Huston, emeritus associate professor of history at Duke University and author of Land and Freedom: Rural Society, Popular Protest, and Party Politics in Antebellum New York; Victoria Kupchinetsky and Misha Gutkin, director and producer of the film Calico Rebellion; David Fleming, the town supervisor of Nassau, NY; Nancy Newman, professor at SUNY Albany and author of the book Songs and Sounds of the Anti-Rent Movement in Upstate New York; and the Association of Public Historians of New York State.

snippet.title: The Battle That Saved Europe: When 2,000 Hungarians Crushed 40,000 Ottomans
snippet.description:
In 1552, the Siege of Eger became one of the most important battles in Hungarian history, as the Ottoman Empire invaded Hungary with over 40,000 soldiers during its expansion into Central Europe. This medieval siege and last stand documentary follows how barely 2,000 Hungarian defenders faced overwhelming odds in a decisive moment of European history.

With no hope of reinforcements and defeat seemingly inevitable, the defenders of Eger turned to ingenuity, discipline, and ruthless determination. Boiling tar, flaming pitch, cannon fire, and relentless counterattacks transformed the fortress walls into a killing ground, where every breach was met with desperate resistance.

This cinematic historical documentary tells the story of one of Europe’s most astonishing last stands — when courage overcame numbers, when ordinary people became warriors, and when a small fortress halted the advance of an empire.

It is the true story of the Siege of Eger — the battle where 2,000 defenders broke the Ottoman war machine and changed the fate of Central Europe.

snippet.description:

On the 5th of July 1601, a Spanish force of about 12’000 men and 50 siege guns arrived at the Dutch town of Ostend. This was the beginning of a war of attrition which was to last for more than three years. Because of its long duration and high rate of casualties this siege became known as New Troy. It was a siege characterized by curious Spectators that were shipped in and out of the city and by ingenious siege craft never seen before, and rarely after. It was also a siege that proved the importance of bookworms. This is how Contemporary historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of Ostend.

snippet.title: New Unit Cohesion Mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3 (Idea)
snippet.description:
A new proposed "Unit Cohesion" mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3. With the War Core engine and the early development stage of the game, I figured it was time to open a discussion on how to improve historical combat for Total War. Link to presentation: https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVGTtlPgE=/?share_link_id=304447018859

The Problem:
Historical battles have stagnated due to low unit variety and limited paths to victory (always hammer and anvil). The binary nature of morale also means that nothing mechanically happens to a unit before it flees, leading to boring and grinding gameplay.

The Solution:
Introduce a new "unit cohesion" mechanic that fundamentally changes a unit's behavior prior to being routed to allow for more unit differentiation and tactical options.

The Definition:
"Unit Cohesion" is the degree to which individuals act as a unit. This is very important for historical accuracy where the armies were indeed made of individuals whose ability to win was dictated by the leader's ability to command and control them properly. In fact, most battles were won or lost based on this cohesion rather than casualties.

How it works:
Each unit will now have a Unit Leader that serves as the anchor of the unit and to which the other soldiers of that unit are magnetized to. The level of cohesion of a unit dictates how efficiently these soldiers follow the orders of the leader. So if you give an order, the leader goes first, followed by the rest of the men in a response time proportional to their cohesion. In terms of movement, cohesion degrades the farther and faster you go. When a unit stops moving, it can regain cohesion. For combat, a unit's cohesion dictates how effectively it can fight an opponent. More cohesion (and other factors) mean you can push other unit back. More cohesion mean you can withstand cavalry charges.  

Micro Cohesion:
We need an ability to customize units to improve their cohesion stats. This should include a way to select a unit leader and also a support staff (officers, musicians, bannermen) who can improve a unit's cohesion. There should be tools to visualize and test cohesion outside of actual battles such as a "Training Ground" mode.

Macro Cohesion:
A battle line now becomes much more fluid and dynamic as each unit's engagement ebbs and flows based on their cohesion. Generals and other abilities can help influence the state of cohesion of their forces. There should also be a cohesion system for unit's within larger formations. This could work like Carthay's Harmony system.

snippet.title: He Took Jerusalem Without War — While Banned by the Pope ⚔️
snippet.description:
For centuries, crusaders bled and died trying to capture Jerusalem.

Then one man did it without fighting a single battle.

This is the true story of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor — a crusader so controversial that the Pope excommunicated him and forbade him from leading a crusade.

In 1228, Frederick sailed east anyway.
Not with massive armies… but with diplomacy, intelligence, and strategy.

Instead of bloodshed, Frederick negotiated directly with Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt, signing a treaty that handed over Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Nazareth peacefully.

Still banned by the Church, Frederick crowned himself King of Jerusalem — without a priest, without permission, and without war.

This cinematic short reveals one of history’s greatest power moves — a conquest achieved against Papal orders and without a single battle.

snippet.title: Medieval Punishments That Were BANNED for Being TOO Cruel "The Breaking Wheel" Pt 2
snippet.description:
This medieval punishment was so horrifying that after ONE execution, the King of France outlawed it forever. The Breaking Wheel (Catherine's Wheel) was considered too cruel even for the Middle Ages.

🔴 In this video, you'll discover:
- What made the Breaking Wheel the ultimate death sentence for 300+ years
- The execution that shocked a king and changed history forever
- Why a 7-year-old girl's trauma ended this brutal practice in France
- The LAST Breaking Wheel execution in 1841 - over 500 years after the ban

The Breaking Wheel (German: Rädern, French: Roue) was a torture and execution method used from antiquity through the Middle Ages into the early modern period by breaking the bones of a criminal or bystander wheel. This video explores the historical documentation of this practice and its eventual prohibition
